title: Cohomology modules of a complex of modules, as a functor on the derived category
statement:
Let $R$ be a ring and let $\operatorname{Mod}_R$ be the abelian category of $R$-modules, with derived category $D(R)=D(\operatorname{Mod}_R)$ [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. For a cochain complex $C=(C^r,d^r:C^r\to C^{r+1})$ of $R$-modules and an integer $i$, the $i$-th cohomology module is the $R$-module

$$
\mathrm H^i(C)=\ker(d^i:C^i\to C^{i+1})/\operatorname{im}(d^{i-1}:C^{i-1}\to C^i),
$$

and a morphism of complexes $f:C\to C'$ induces the $R$-linear map $\mathrm H^i(f):\mathrm H^i(C)\to\mathrm H^i(C')$, $[x]\mapsto[f^i(x)]$; this is a functor from the category of cochain complexes of $R$-modules to $\operatorname{Mod}_R$. A quasi-isomorphism is by definition a morphism $f$ for which every $\mathrm H^i(f)$ is an isomorphism, so by the universal property of the localization the functor $\mathrm H^i$ factors uniquely through the localization functor $Q$ of complexes to $D(R)$: there is a functor

$$
\mathrm H^i:D(R)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Mod}_R
$$

with $\mathrm H^i\circ Q\cong\mathrm H^i$ (the cohomology of a representing complex), canonically. Hence for an object $C$ of $D(R)$ the module $\mathrm H^i(C)$ is well defined up to canonical isomorphism as the cohomology of any complex representing $C$, and a morphism of $D(R)$ induces an $R$-linear map on $\mathrm H^i$.
